lead: The maximum likelihood estimate is the parameter value that makes the observed sample most likely. You write the chance of the data as a function of the unknown parameter, then choose the value that maximises it. The method turns estimation into a calculus problem: differentiate, set to zero, solve. It works for Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, exponential and normal models, and it extends to regression and machine learning. Engineers use it to fit failure rates, click probabilities and noise variances from data. This chapter shows the likelihood, the log-likelihood and the check that the answer is a maximum.
prereq: You need: expectation and variance (Unit 2), the standard distributions (Unit 3), derivatives from calculus, and Chapter 5.4 on unbiased and consistent estimators.

blocks.text: Let x₁, x₂, …, xₙ be observed values from a distribution with unknown parameter θ. The pmf or pdf at one value is f(x; θ): a probability for discrete data, a density for continuous data. The likelihood treats the data as fixed and θ as variable: L(θ) = Π f(xᵢ; θ), where Π means product. In the discrete case use P(X = xᵢ; θ) in place of f(xᵢ; θ). L(θ) is not the probability of θ. It is the chance of seeing this sample, viewed as a function of θ. The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) θ̂ is the value that maximises L(θ). Products are awkward to differentiate, so use the log-likelihood ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ). Because ln is increasing, L and ℓ peak at the same θ. Differentiate ℓ, set dℓ/dθ = 0, solve, and check d²ℓ/dθ² < 0 at the root or check the boundary.
L(θ) = Πᵢ₌₁ⁿ f(xᵢ; θ),   ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ) = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ ln f(xᵢ; θ)
blocks.where: θ is the unknown parameter; x₁,…,xₙ are the observed values; f(xᵢ; θ) is the pmf or pdf at xᵢ; Π is the product over i = 1 to n; Σ is the sum over i = 1 to n.

items: Write L(θ) as a product over all observations.
Take ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ). Drop additive constants that do not depend on θ when you only need the maximiser.
Differentiate ℓ with respect to θ.
Set dℓ/dθ = 0 and solve for θ.
Check d²ℓ/dθ² < 0 at the solution, or compare with the boundary values when θ has limits.

blocks.text: Invariance: if θ̂ is the MLE of θ and g is a function, then g(θ̂) is the MLE of g(θ). For example, if λ̂ is the MLE of a Poisson rate λ, then the MLE of 1/λ is 1/λ̂. This saves work when a question asks for a transformed parameter. A boundary answer can occur: for p in [0, 1], the maximum of L(p) may be at p = 0 or p = 1 if all trials are failures or all are successes. The same steps work for discrete and continuous models.
Let x̄ = (1/n) Σ xᵢ be the sample mean. The list gives standard one-parameter or two-parameter MLEs.

items: Bernoulli(p): p̂ = x̄, the fraction of successes in 0/1 data.
Exponential(rate λ): λ̂ = 1/x̄; the mean is 1/λ.
Normal(μ, σ²): μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = (1/n) Σ (xᵢ − x̄)². The divisor is n, not n − 1.

blocks.text: The normal variance MLE is biased: E[σ̂²] = σ²(n − 1)/n, so it underestimates σ² on average. An MLE can be biased even when it is consistent. Bias is judged separately; see Chapter 5.4. In large samples the bias becomes small. The unbiased estimator S² = (1/(n−1)) Σ (xᵢ − x̄)² is not the MLE of σ², but it is often preferred in small samples. For the Bernoulli model, p̂ = x̄ is unbiased; for the Poisson model, λ̂ = x̄ is also unbiased.

examples.question: In 10 independent UPI payment attempts on a slow network, 7 succeed. Model the number of successes as Binomial(10, p). Find the maximum likelihood estimate of p. Show the likelihood, log-likelihood, derivative and second-derivative check.
steps: Let X ~ Binomial(n = 10, p). The observed value is x = 7. The likelihood for this observation is L(p) = C(10,7) p⁷ (1−p)³, where C(10,7) = 120 is the binomial coefficient.
The constant 120 does not depend on p. Maximising L(p) is the same as maximising p⁷ (1−p)³.
Log-likelihood: ℓ(p) = ln 120 + 7 ln p + 3 ln(1−p), for 0 < p < 1.
Set dℓ/dp = 0: 7/p = 3/(1−p). Cross multiply: 7(1−p) = 3p, so 7 − 7p = 3p, 7 = 10p, and p̂ = 0.7.
Second derivative: d²ℓ/dp² = −7/p² − 3/(1−p)². At p = 0.7 this is −7/0.49 − 3/0.09 = −14.2857 − 33.3333 = −47.6190, which is negative, so p = 0.7 is a maximum.
examples.answer: The maximum likelihood estimate is p̂ = 0.7, so the estimated success probability is 0.7 (70%).

traps: Confusing likelihood with the probability of θ. L(θ) is the chance of the observed data as a function of θ, not a probability distribution over θ.
Dropping a factor that depends on θ. You may drop constants and additive terms in ℓ, but not a term such as p⁷ or (1−p)³.
Setting the derivative to zero without checking the second derivative or the boundary. A stationary point can be a minimum, and the maximum can be at p = 0 or p = 1.
Using n − 1 in the normal variance MLE. The MLE divides by n; the unbiased estimator divides by n − 1.
Assuming every MLE is unbiased. The normal variance MLE is biased downward.

quiz.q: Write the likelihood for a sample x₁,…,xₙ from a distribution with pdf f(x; θ).
Why is the log-likelihood used instead of the likelihood when finding an MLE?
quiz.a: ln is increasing, so the maximiser is the same. The log turns a product into a sum, which is easier to differentiate and less prone to numerical underflow.

quiz.q: A Poisson sample has values 2, 3, 4, 5. Find the MLE of λ.
quiz.a: x̄ = (2+3+4+5)/4 = 14/4 = 3.5, so λ̂ = 3.5 events per unit interval.

quiz.q: A normal sample has n = 5 and Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² = 20. Find the MLE of σ² and the unbiased estimate. Which is larger?
quiz.a: MLE σ̂² = 20/5 = 4. Unbiased S² = 20/4 = 5. S² is larger because the MLE divides by n and is biased downward.

quiz.q: State the invariance property of MLEs.
quiz.a: If θ̂ is the MLE of θ, then g(θ̂) is the MLE of g(θ).

quiz.q: An exponential sample has mean x̄ = 4 minutes. Find the MLE of the rate λ and the MLE of the mean 1/λ.
quiz.a: λ̂ = 1/x̄ = 1/4 = 0.25 per minute. The MLE of the mean is 1/λ̂ = 4 minutes.

quiz.q: Give an example of an MLE that is biased and explain why it is still used.
quiz.a: For a normal sample, σ̂² = (1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)² is biased: E[σ̂²] = σ²(n−1)/n. It is still used because it is the MLE, it is consistent, and in large samples the bias is small.

beyond: Not for the exam. Maximum likelihood is the default fitting method in modern statistics and machine learning. Logistic regression, hidden Markov models and many neural-network losses are likelihood or log-likelihood objectives. When the derivative has no closed form, software uses numerical optimisation such as Newton–Raphson or gradient descent. The EM algorithm handles missing data and latent variables by alternating expectation and maximisation steps. Search next for 'logistic regression maximum likelihood', 'EM algorithm' and 'Fisher information'.
